zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Review reference: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics (NINJAL), Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510; CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The supplied lexical index was consulted as a secondary aid; the transcription and English review notes are scan-based reviewer work, not a reproduction of that dataset.

lines.note: Nomikomi is swallowing. It also confirms that the preceding page's Nomi- is a catchword, not an additional body entry; the printed ôda principal form is retained.

Nomikuzushi introduces a usage discussion rather than a simple equivalent. The dictionary says that, although a dialogue uses the verb in one sense, a different causative or transitive use is more proper; the doubled zz is visible.

runs.text: està por beber deſordenadamente de maneira q̃

lines.note: Continues the reported dialogue usage: drinking excessively or disorderly to such a degree that something follows. The row is physically indented like the surrounding explanation, correcting the draft's unindented placement.

runs.text: hum estrague o eſtamago, ou as entranhas, não

lines.note: Specifies injuring one's stomach or entrails through that drinking. Eſtamago is the printed historical vowel spelling, not silently replaced by estomago; the continuation indentation is restored.

runs.text: he proprio modo de falar; mais propriamente

lines.note: Rejects the preceding use as not the proper expression and introduces a preferable use. A semicolon, not a comma, follows falar; the physical continuation is indented.

runs.text: ſe dirà de quem faz beber a outros atè mais

lines.note: Says the verb is more properly used of someone who makes other people drink. The mark in atè is a grave stroke, not the OCR tilde; 'until they can no longer ...' continues below.

runs.text: não poder fazendo os aleuantar do Zaxiqui.

lines.note: Completes the preferred sense: making others drink beyond their capacity and rise from the reception room. Zaxiqui is Japanese zashiki within the Portuguese explanation; its full italic word is retained and tagged, replacing the draft's isolated roman Z. The row is indented.
Nomihatashi means finishing drinking. The printed h-row f and the historical aita principal form are preserved.
Nomihoshi means drinking everything up. The following continuation specifies leaving nothing, distinguishing the exhaustive sense from merely finishing an occasion of drinking.
Completes 'without leaving anything'. The short word closes the Nomifoxi entry and is not a catchword.

Nomiire is illustrated by nomiirebuta, an inset lid. Enlargement shows two dotted i types in both forms, correcting Nomire/Nomirebuta; the separate i vowels belong to the compound rather than a length mark.

runs.text: çapadoura que ſe mete em caixa de maneira que

lines.note: Describes a cover fitted into a box. The first word looks unusual beside expected tapadoura, but the supplied çapadoura is supported by the low c-shaped body and visible descending mark and is retained as a printed anomaly. The continuation indentation is restored.

runs.text: parece hũa ſoo couſa com a caixa, ou boceta.

lines.note: The fitted lid appears to be a single object with the box or small container. The print's hũa ſoo and boceta are retained without modernizing the spelling.
The related verb nomiire means swallowing or gulping down. Both i types are present in the headword, as in the inset-lid entry above; ruru is the printed inflectional continuation.

runs.text: ¶ Item, per met. Entender, & perceber bẽ

lines.note: Introduces a metaphorical sense of understanding and perceiving well. Per met. is explanatory apparatus, and the nasal abbreviation in bẽ is retained.
Completes the metaphorical object: understanding something. The row belongs to the swallowing/understanding entry, not the following sword-fitting entry.

runs.text: Certo ferro, ou metal que poẽ

lines.note: Nomiire habaki names a metal sword fitting, specified more fully below. Enlarged comparison and the supplied NINJAL index support Nomiire, with the second i and r, rather than OCR Nomite; the index is used only as a lexical cross-check.

runs.text: ſobre a Catana dobrado de baixo da empunha-

lines.note: Places the folded metal on the sword beneath the hilt. Catana is a Japanese-derived sword term embedded in the Portuguese description and is tagged as a whole word; the printed empunha-dura division and continuation indentation are retained.

runs.text: dura onde justa a bainha com os punhos.

lines.note: Completes empunhadura and identifies the place where the sheath fits against the hilt. Justa is preserved as printed rather than expanded to ajusta; the baseline st classification is not globally revised.
Nomi narazu means 'not only, but also'. The printed joining is retained, while the gloss identifies its connective function rather than a drinking verb.
Nomisonji is equated with nomisokono, failing to drink. The long s types and the caron in the alternative form are visible; the explanatory Portuguese begins on the next row.

runs.text: Não poder beber, ou deixar de beber por al-

lines.note: Gives inability to drink, or omitting to drink for some reason. The visible al- begins alguma on the following row; the initial capital does not make this a separate entry.

Completes 'for some reason' and begins a conditional example, moshi mata nomisonzuru ni oite wa. The printed hyphen separates the following particle environment, without authorizing an inserted vowel or changed inflection.
Continues 'in the event that [I fail], all the wealth of my household ...'. Icqeno is ikka no, not a malformed personal name; its cq and the circumflex in zaifôuo are retained.

Completes the pledge to give the wealth as a payment or forfeit. Fab. is the upright fable citation; the Portuguese begins 'and if by chance'. No terminal hyphen is visible after poruentu, so none is supplied despite its continuation below.

runs.text: ra não poder beber todo o mar, toda minha ri-

lines.note: Completes porventura and states the condition of being unable to drink the whole sea. Ri- visibly divides riqueza, the wealth pledged in the consequence.

runs.text: queza vos darei por peita: esta palaura ainda

lines.note: Completes the promise to give all the wealth as peita. After the colon the lexicographers begin another usage caveat; the printed esta is not silently accented or otherwise regularized.

runs.text: que esta em exemplo das fabulas não ſe vſa

lines.note: Acknowledges that the word occurs in an example from the fables, but says it is not normally used in that sense. The source distinguishes attestation from ordinary accepted usage.
Finishes the warning that the quoted sense is not customary. This closes the lengthy Nomisonji entry rather than qualifying the next headword.
Nomitsukushi means exhausting a supply by drinking it. The printed uita principal form and long s in the gloss are retained without normalization.

runs.text: Bebedor, ou o que bebe muito vinho.

lines.note: Nomite is a drinker, explained as someone who drinks much wine. This genuine -te noun contrasts with the earlier Nomiire forms that the OCR had misread.
Nomiyoi denotes becoming drunk. The example begins the divided tachimachi ni, 'immediately'; both long-o inflection marks are circumflexes.
Continues 'immediately becoming drunk and lowering his head'. Caxira wo is the object phrase, and zo links to the following classical predicate; no spaces are inserted into the printed joined forms.

Completes the classical predicate 'lay down'. The source label visibly reads Tai., without a securely printed additional letter; Book 26 follows in italic. Em- begins the Portuguese embebedando-se across the row boundary.

Completes becoming drunk and lowering the head. The terminal mark after ſe is printed and is retained even though modern prose would separate the pronoun from the following verb without such a line-end mark.
Finishes the translation, 'lay down'. This single-word row is part of the quotation and has its own complete crop.

runs.text: O que guarda os campos, ou tem cui-

lines.note: Nomori is a keeper of fields or someone charged with their care. Cui- visibly continues into cuidado on the next row.
Completes care of the greenery and woodland or grazing land. The Portuguese gives a land-management explanation without naming a particular official office.

runs.text: Nomorino cagami. i, Noni aru mizzu.

lines.note: Nomori no kagami, literally the field-keeper's mirror, is equated with water in the fields. The printed mizzu preserves the dictionary's consonant distinction and is not modernized to mizu.

Gives 'water of the fields' and labels the expression poetic with P. The capital C in Campos and the locally slanted appearance of the final P. are retained. Comparison with the upright P. in column 2 leaves this small label a nonblocking typeface caveat, rather than grounds for global regularization.
Nomose is explained by no no omote, the surface of the field. The Japanese spelling xe corresponds to se in the reading; the tilde and terminal hyphen in cã- are both visible.

Completes campo and marks the expression as poetic. The short continuation and the draft’s italic P. are retained after comparison with line 40; the small label shares its nonblocking typeface caveat. No missing substantive gloss is inferred.
Nonin is a farmer, paraphrased by mono-tsukuri. The Japanese synonym is not an embedded term inside Portuguese prose; la- begins the gloss's verb lavrar across the row boundary.
Completes 'who tills or cultivates the fields'. The historical la-ura spelling division is retained exactly, rather than replaced by modern lavra.

runs.text: Voz com que ſe chama por alguem,

lines.note: Nono is an attention-getting call addressed to someone. Both marks over o point downward in the scan and are transcribed as carons, correcting the first circumflex in the draft.
Compares the Japanese call to saying oula, oula. This is the dictionary's Portuguese interjectional comparison, not an instruction to normalize the Japanese vowels.
Nonomeki denotes bustle, commotion, or noisy activity. The last fa- continues with zerſe at the top of column 2, establishing the column-to-column reading order.
Completes fazer-se from the bottom of column 1: a great bustle, disturbance, or commotion takes place. The initial zerſe is continuation text, not a headword or a repeated catchword.
Nonoshiri is speaking abusively with noise or clamour. The Portuguese continues with threats and boasting, and the printed itta principal form is retained.

runs.text: & ameaças, ou dizendo bem deſi, & vãa

lines.note: Adds threats, or praising oneself and vain-glorying. The printed deſi is joined, while vãa begins the expression completed by gloriando below; neither is modernized.

Completes the boastful conduct as scorning other people. The scan joins desdanhar into one word, correcting des danhar, but its historical a vowel is preserved rather than replaced by modern desdenhar.
Nonki is recreation or relaxation. The example nonki wo suru gives the corresponding activity, rather than the later evaluative sense of being careless.
Translates nonki wo suru as taking recreation. The brief row is a complete example translation, not omitted headword text.

runs.text: feſta, ou banquete que ſe faz com

lines.note: Nonrio denotes a feast or banquet associated with a move. The lower-case initial of feſta and the final caron in the Japanese headword are preserved from the print.

runs.text: a noua mudança pera outra camara.

lines.note: Specifies moving into another chamber or room. This completes the occasion for the feast without asserting a more specific modern ceremonial identification.
Nonseki is glossed as a tatami or straw mattress. The scan supports Tatami, correcting Taiami; Tatami is a whole Japanese word embedded in Portuguese prose and is tagged for typeface review.

runs.text: Meſtre, ou guia nas couſas da ſalua-

lines.note: Noke is a teacher or guide in matters of salvation. The headword's long-o circumflex distinguishes it from the following unaccented verb Noqe; ſalua- is visibly divided.
Completes salvação and adds guidance in learning or letters. The wording broadens the teacher's field beyond religious instruction alone.
Noke is moving something aside or separating it. The unusual space in a partar is visibly present and retained, unlike the spurious space in the later Afaſtarſe entry.

runs.text: Modo de pelejar com a cabeça

lines.note: Noke-kabuto denotes fighting with the head held back or raised. The following explanation treats that posture as a sign of fear or weakening, rather than bravery.

runs.text: erguida que he geito de temer, ou enfraquecer.

lines.note: Explains the raised-head posture as the manner of someone afraid or losing strength. Geito and the rest of the historical Portuguese spelling remain unmodernized.
Gives noke kabuto ni tatako, fighting in that posture. The visible space inside the compound and the caron in tatacǒ are preserved; its Portuguese translation continues below.

runs.text: o capacete, & cabeça alta. i, Com geito de

lines.note: Translates the posture as helmet and head held high, then begins a clarifying explanation. The i, belongs to the explanatory apparatus, not a Japanese particle.
Completes the clarification as appearing likely to be defeated or afraid. This closes the posture entry rather than predicting an actual outcome.

Noket is the checked-coda form for pus and blood, explicitly paraphrased as umi, chi. Separate second-pass enlargement confirms a slanted italic initial V beside upright mi; this mixed printing is preserved. The whole word is nevertheless Japanese umi, regardless of the fallible kana hint's font-based segmentation.

runs.text: Borda do telhado que ſae pera fora.

lines.note: Noki is the projecting edge of a roof, the eaves. The definition is complete on this row and distinct from the following homophonous verb.
Noki is moving or withdrawing oneself aside. Afaſtarſe is visibly one word, correcting the draft's A faſtarſe; its long s is preserved.

runs.text: Taboa como ripa, que ſe poem

lines.note: Nokitsuke is described as a board like a lath. The following rows explain where it is fixed and what it holds, so the gloss is about roofing construction rather than a general plank.

runs.text: na borda do telhado pera ter mão nas taboinhas

lines.note: Places the lath at the roof edge to hold the small boards in place. Ter mão nas expresses keeping hold of them; the printed diminutive taboinhas is retained.
Identifies those small boards as the pieces serving as roof tiles or shingles. This completes the function of the edge lath.

runs.text: Pao que atraueſa de baixo da bor-

lines.note: Nokigeta is the timber running underneath the eaves. The single long s in atraueſa is retained from the print, and bor- continues into borda below.
Completes borda do telhado, placing the timber underneath the roof edge. The row belongs to Noqigueta and carries no separate headword.
Nokiguchi names the edges or eaves of the roof. The plural Portuguese gloss is kept rather than merged with the preceding structural timber entry.
Nora is equated with nobara, open country or a field. The initial of Nobara is a clear N, not OCR X; the final upright P. marks poetic usage and is separated from the italic gloss.
Noran is paraphrased through suffering and becoming disordered. The Portuguese begins disturbance or agitation, and the headword visibly has a caron rather than a circumflex.

runs.text: ou inquietação cauſada dalgũa dor, ou tra-

lines.note: Explains the disturbance as uneasiness caused by some pain or trouble. The tilde in dalgũa and the physical tra-balho division are retained.
Completes trabalho, here trouble or suffering. This closes the Noran definition and does not begin the curtain entry below.
Noren is a curtain. Noren wo kakuru is the example of putting up or hanging curtains, translated on the next row.
Gives placing or suspending curtains. The next example starts with a visible hyphen after Noren and continues into uo taruru below; Por has no supplied accent.
Completes the second Japanese curtain example and its gloss, curtains being in place and hanging. The printed taruru is retained rather than replaced by a modern verb form.
Completes 'suspended'. This single-word continuation closes the second Noren example.

runs.text: Deſfazerſe, ou abrirſe com dor, me-

lines.note: Noret is a checked-coda noun or expression for being torn apart or broken open by pain or fear. The print distinguishes the successive long s and f in Deſfazerſe; me- begins medo below.
Completes medo, fear, followed by the printed abbreviation for further causes. It belongs to the preceding emotional or painful rupture description.

Nori means law or religious teaching. The gloss visibly reads italic Ley, correcting the garbled mixed-type Leg; nori wo hiromuru means spreading that teaching, with Dila-tar divided at the right edge.
Completes spreading the law and adds expounding or preaching it. The final mark after ley is a period, not a hyphen; the grave accent in Prègar is retained.

runs.text: Grude feito de arroz moido com agoa,

lines.note: This Nori is adhesive paste made from rice ground with water. It is a separate homophone, not another religious sense.
Adds that the rice-and-water mixture is cooked over a fire. This completes the method of making the paste as described by the dictionary.
This Nori is a measure of distance. The scan supports Quantidade, correcting Quamidade; Michi- begins the example about the length of a road.
Completes michi no nori go-ri nari, stating that the road is five ri long. The Portuguese renders the unit by legoas on the following row, without establishing a modern conversion factor.
Completes 'five leagues', the dictionary's translation of go-ri. No numerical equivalence to a modern kilometer measure is inferred.
Begins the verb noru, getting up or mounting. Its initial N aligns with the other headwords, so the draft's continuation indentation is removed; the first figurative example divides no-ru visibly.

runs.text: ru. l, rini noru. l, qini noru.

lines.note: Completes katsu ni noru and adds ri ni noru and ki ni noru as alternative expressions. The lower-case l markers mean 'or'; the Portuguese begins taking courage or confidence.

runs.text: animo, & ouſadia com a victoria, ou com

lines.note: Explains gaining spirit and boldness through victory. The clause continues with another condition of gaining the upper hand on the next row.

runs.text: ficar de cima em algũa couſa. ¶

lines.note: Completes taking confidence from superiority in some matter and starts uma ni, 'on a horse'. The separate noru at the bottom repeats the opening word of f371 and is a catchword; the running example continues on that next page.
